summary:
What We Left Behind is a bilingual (English and Arabic) interactive storybook for children about the machines humanity has left on other worlds.

It features two stories: on the Moon, children discover objects left by astronauts, including the Lunar Roving Vehicle, and learn why they remain there. On Mars, a curious child befriends NASA’s Opportunity rover, designed for 90 days but which explored for almost 15 years.

Each page combines illustrations, professional narration in both languages, mini-games, drag-and-drop activities, and fact cards introducing real NASA science. Children learn through play, such as moving a calendar to experience six weeks of rover activity.

The book turns mission history into an emotional, interactive experience. It also gives Arabic-speaking children greater access to space science in their language. At only 23 MB, it works offline on phones and computers, making it accessible to schools and families with limited internet.

Future Plans: We aim to add voice recognition for blind and visually impaired students, allowing them to use commands like "next page" and "read to me" without touching the screen. We also plan to add more bilingual, narrated, and interactive stories about rovers, spacecraft, and other space exploration missions.
details:
What it does and how it works

What We Left Behind is an interactive, bilingual storybook for school students. It tells two true stories about the vehicles people have left in space. In the first, Leen discovers the three Lunar Roving Vehicles that the Apollo 15, 16 and 17 crews left parked on the Moon. In the second, Leo follows NASA’s Opportunity rover across Mars, from its landing in 2004 to its last message in 2018.

The book has 36 illustrated pages, and every page asks the reader to do something:

fold the lunar rover with a slider so it fits inside the lander;

drag a calendar and watch six weeks pass as Opportunity climbs out of Victoria Crater;

press “Send signal” to try to reach Opportunity from Earth, as NASA did in 2018.

All 642 lines of the story are narrated in Arabic and English, and an auto-read mode lets younger readers follow along by listening. Both stories end on the challenge’s own question: is what we left behind space junk, or a treasure of history? The book sets out both sides, protecting landing sites like museums or worrying about debris mixing with science samples, and lets students decide. The last page lists the team’s five NASA sources as APA citations.

Benefits

Works anywhere: the whole book is one 23 MB web file. It runs in any modern browser on a phone or computer, with no app, installation, account or internet connection after the download.

Arabic and English equally: every word, voice and button exists in both languages, so Arabic-reading students get a space story as rich as an English one.

For every kind of reader: narration and auto-read support younger students and those still building reading skills.

Learning by doing: students touch, drag and explore space history instead of memorising names and dates.

Intended impact

We want students to know that Apollo rovers are still parked on the Moon and that Opportunity rests on Mars, and to care about what happens to them. Beyond facts, we want students to practise thinking: to weigh two real arguments about space heritage and space debris and form their own opinion. Because it is free, offline and bilingual, the book can reach classrooms with weak internet, old devices or few Arabic science resources.

Tools, languages and software

Code: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks or dependencies.

Build: PowerShell scripts that pack all code, pictures, voices and fonts into a single, locked, view-only HTML file.

Media: images compressed to WebP, and narration encoded as Ogg Opus at 18 kbps, to keep the book under 25 MB.

Voice: narration was generated with AI text-to-speech (ElevenLabs). We then checked it by transcription and corrected Arabic misreadings by adjusting diacritics.

Fonts: free, open-licence fonts saved inside the book: Fredoka for English, Baloo Bhaijaan 2 and Readex Pro for Arabic.

Science: NASA mission sources for every fact in the story.

How it is creative

Two stories, one question: a Moon story and a Mars story mirror each other and meet at the same challenge question.

Every page is a small game tied to a real event, such as the 2018 signal attempts or the rover folding into the lander.

The Omani look: one optional button turns Leo into Hassan, with his own recorded voice lines in both languages. It also dresses the children in a dishdasha, kumma and embroidered dress, raises an Omani flag on the Moon, swaps in a cover painted by the team, and adds a dallah, dates and a mabkhara to the home scenes. The story and science stay the same, so a student can see themselves in a real space story. The idea can be repeated for any culture.

Sticker-style art gives every character, rover and planet a friendly face that suits young readers.

Factors the team considered

Accuracy: every fact is checked against NASA sources, and the challenge question is presented with both views and no single “right” answer.

Language and culture: full Arabic support, with correct right-to-left layout and narration, plus optional Omani representation.

Access: works offline on low-end phones, needs no account or internet, and fits in one small file.

Age-appropriate design: large buttons, read-aloud, short text on each page and hands-on interactions.

Privacy: no sign-ups, tracking or data collection.

Protecting our work: the downloadable book is view-only and locked against editing.
